title: Should You Apply to FAST With an NTS NAT or SAT Score Instead?
excerpt: FAST doesn't require you to sit its own entry test — NTS NAT and SAT scores are accepted too. Here's how the alternatives actually work, and why the seat math changes your odds more than most students realize.

content.text: FAST's own test isn't your only route in

A lot of students assume that applying to FAST means sitting FAST's own NU Entry Test, full stop. In reality, FAST accepts three different ways to satisfy the entry test requirement: its own NU Test, an NTS NAT score (NAT-IE for engineering, NAT-ICS or NAT-ICOM for computing and business programs respectively), or a qualifying SAT score. Whichever route you use, your merit is calculated the same way — the same 10% Matric + 40% FSc + 50% test-score formula applies regardless of which test supplied that 50%.

This matters most for two groups: overseas Pakistanis who can't travel back to sit the on-campus NU Test, and students who've already invested in SAT or NTS prep for other university applications and don't want to duplicate effort with a third, FAST-specific exam.

FAST does not accept ECAT as a substitute — only its own NU Test, NTS NAT, or SAT qualify. Confirm current accepted test types and any minimum score requirements directly at nu.edu.pk before deciding which route to take, since policies here have been updated in recent cycles.
The seat math you need to know before choosing this route

Here's the detail that changes the calculation for a lot of students: seats aren't split evenly across these three routes. The NU Test pathway carries the large majority of available seats, while the NTS/SAT route is generally reported to draw from a much smaller allocation — commonly cited as somewhere around 5-10% of total seats. Because fewer seats are competing for that route but a meaningful number of strong-scoring applicants still apply through it, the effective merit cutoff on the NTS/SAT quota tends to run noticeably higher than on the main NU Test merit list — some sources point to NTS scores needing to be in the 90s to be genuinely competitive.

The exact seat allocation and cutoff gap between the NU Test and NTS/SAT routes can vary by campus and year — this hasn't been independently confirmed against FAST's own published seat-allocation numbers. Treat this as a real, worth-checking consideration rather than a fixed rule, and verify current seat splits at nu.edu.pk before ruling either route in or out.
Why this doesn't mean "avoid NTS/SAT entirely"

None of this means the alternative routes aren't worth using — it means they shouldn't be your default plan if the NU Test is realistically available to you. If you're a Pakistan-based FSc student who can sit the on-campus test, prioritizing the NU Test generally gives you access to the larger seat pool and a comparatively less crowded merit list. If you're overseas, doing A-Levels, or already hold a strong SAT or NTS score from other applications, the alternative route stops being a "smaller pool, harder odds" tradeoff and becomes simply the only realistic way in — in which case it's absolutely worth using.

items: Prioritize the NU Test if: you're in Pakistan, doing FSc, and can sit the on-campus exam without major logistical barriers
Use NTS NAT if: you already have a strong NAT score from other university applications and want to avoid sitting a second, separate exam
Use SAT if: you're an overseas applicant, doing an international curriculum, or already have a competitive SAT score built for other purposes

content.text: Historically, some sources have cited informal minimum SAT benchmarks — around 1200 for CS/Engineering programs and 1000 for BBA-track programs — but more recent guidance suggests FAST has moved toward a purely merit-based system without a hard minimum score, similar to how NTS cutoffs are decided by where the merit list actually lands rather than a fixed published number. This is exactly the kind of detail that shifts between cycles, so treat any specific minimum score you see quoted online, including the numbers above, as historical context rather than the current rule.

Confirm current SAT and NTS score requirements — including whether a fixed minimum still applies at all — directly on FAST's official eligibility criteria page before finalizing which test to prepare for or submit.
If your FSc result isn't out yet

If you're applying before your FSc Part 2 result is announced, some guidance indicates FAST substitutes your Matric percentage, adjusted by a conversion factor, in place of the missing FSc component for that portion of the aggregate. This detail hasn't been independently verified from more than one source in this research pass, so it's worth confirming directly with FAST's admissions office or the official FAQ page if this situation applies to you, rather than assuming a specific formula.

If you're eligible to sit FAST's own NU Test without real logistical difficulty, that's generally the stronger default given the larger seat pool. The NTS/SAT route is a genuinely valuable option — not a fallback to be embarrassed about — for overseas applicants, A-Level students, or anyone who's already built a strong score through other applications and wants that effort to count here too. Either way, the one universal rule is the same: confirm current accepted score types, any minimum thresholds, and seat allocations directly with FAST before locking in your strategy, since this is one of the areas of their admission policy that appears to shift between cycles more than most.

items.question: Does FAST accept ECAT as a substitute for its entry test?
items.answer: No. FAST only accepts its own NU Test, an NTS NAT score, or a qualifying SAT score — ECAT is not accepted as a substitute.

items.question: Does the merit formula change if I use an NTS or SAT score instead of FAST's own test?
items.answer: No. The same 10% Matric + 40% FSc + 50% test-score formula applies regardless of which of the three accepted tests supplied that 50%.

items.question: Is it harder to get in through the NTS/SAT route than through FAST's own NU Test?
items.answer: It can be. The NTS/SAT route is generally reported to draw from a much smaller seat allocation than the NU Test pathway, which tends to push its effective merit cutoff higher — though exact seat splits vary by campus and year and should be confirmed with FAST directly.

items.question: Is there a minimum SAT or NTS score required to apply to FAST?
items.answer: This isn't fully settled — some sources cite historical minimums (around 1200 for CS/Engineering, 1000 for BBA), while more recent guidance suggests FAST has moved to a purely merit-based system with no fixed cutoff. Confirm the current requirement on FAST's official eligibility page before relying on either figure.

items.question: Who should consider using NTS NAT or SAT instead of FAST's own test?
items.answer: Mainly overseas applicants who can't sit the on-campus NU Test, and students who already hold a strong SAT or NTS score from other university applications and want to avoid preparing for a third, FAST-specific exam.
